items.title: Simon Willison builds Beep Locator with Claude to triangulate a mysterious beep using multiple devices and Python web server [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.summary:
Simon Willison developed Beep Locator, a software system that uses multiple devices scattered around a room to triangulate the source of an intermittent beep. The system runs a Python web server coordinating devices like phones, tablets, and laptops that listen for beeps, estimate their locations, and display the results on a map, enabling identification of the beep's source within about 40 centimeters.

Beep Locator is based on a 2007 research paper called BeepBeep, which uses acoustic ranging with commodity hardware. The system records audio buffers, detects beeps using Fast Fourier Transform, and aligns audio clips via a chirp signal to locate the beep. Simon used Claude Code to build and iteratively improve the system, adding features like rough device positioning, clap testing, sound replay, and automatic beep frequency recognition.

This project demonstrates how AI coding agents like Claude can be given "ears" by running code that analyzes audio input from multiple devices, enabling autonomous problem-solving and live software updates without manual intervention on each device.

items.originalSummary:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

items.title: Notion discloses Fireworks AI security breach exposed unattributable AI chat transcripts affecting under 1% of workspaces [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
items.summary:
Notion reported a security incident involving its third-party AI vendor Fireworks AI, which may have exposed unattributable Notion AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces. The exposed data did not include identifiable workspace, user, or company information, and no other workspace data was affected.

Notion used Fireworks AI for classification tasks and serving open-weight models within its product, but has since disabled the affected Insights feature, disconnected from Fireworks, and deleted related data. Affected workspace owners have been notified and can securely review the exposed data, while Notion recommends rotating any sensitive credentials that may have been shared during the incident period.

The company continues to monitor the situation and has halted all training runs involving Fireworks AI to prevent further exposure.

items.title: CoreWeave bond yield rises above 16% amid increasing credit stress in AI infrastructure sector [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
items.summary:
CoreWeave's 2032 bond yield has climbed above 16%, reflecting investor concerns about financing the AI infrastructure boom as credit default swap costs rise across AI-linked companies like Nvidia, Broadcom, and Oracle. This increase signals higher financing costs and growing market caution despite ongoing substantial borrowing to fund AI expansion.

Credit markets have been unsettled by political challenges, including potential moratoriums on data center projects in key states governed by Democrats, which could impact nearly half of planned U.S. AI data center capacity. Despite these concerns, AI-related debt issuance remains robust, with Goldman Sachs forecasting continued high levels of borrowing by hyperscalers through 2027.

The main uncertainty now is how quickly AI spending will generate sufficient cash flow to satisfy investors amid rising capital expenditures and negative free cash flow reported by hyperscalers. Analysts warn that any slowdown in AI infrastructure projects due to political or market pressures could reduce capital spending and debt issuance in the near future.

items.title: Wired profiles spouses of AI workers facing emotional strain and family challenges amid the AI boom in the Bay Area [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Meet the Sad Wives of AI
items.summary:
An article explores the emotional and social impact of the AI industry on the spouses of AI professionals, focusing on the Bay Area where many partners feel neglected or overwhelmed by their significant others' intense focus on AI work. It highlights the gender imbalance in AI roles and the resulting household dynamics, with many women expressing frustration and fatigue as AI dominates conversations and priorities.

The piece includes personal accounts from spouses who have relocated for AI careers or live with partners deeply immersed in AI development, describing the toll on relationships and social life. Experts note that this phenomenon reflects broader labor market shifts and historical patterns where technological booms reshape family roles and expectations.

The article suggests that the AI boom is not only a technological revolution but also a social one, affecting family dynamics and mental health, with many spouses seeking recognition and balance amid the relentless pace of AI innovation.

items.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators despite earlier privacy promises [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
items.summary:
Google has updated its Gemini Workspace extensions to allow personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive to be routed to human reviewers, reversing its 2023 promise that such data would not be seen by humans. Testing shows that this data ingestion happens automatically during conversations without explicit user commands, with varying levels of data exposure from summaries to full unredacted files.

The updated Google Help documentation and blog post warn users not to connect apps containing confidential information to Gemini Apps, as human reviewers may access this data. Google's automatic data scrubbers are insufficient to fully deidentify sensitive information, raising privacy concerns about the handling of personal content in Gemini Workspace integrations.

items.originalTitle: Muse Ember: Our smallest, most efficient model
items.summary:

It delivers comparable or better intelligence than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna at significantly lower cost, positioning it on the efficiency frontier for AI reasoning workloads.

Muse Ember supports a 1 million token context window and multimodal inputs including text, images, audio, and video, enabling it to handle large codebases, documents, and multimedia content in a single call. Early testing by partners highlighted its speed, accuracy, and token efficiency in tasks like contract review, candidate screening, and coding, making it suitable for enterprise agent workflows and engineering teams.

The model is available on the Meta Model API with pricing at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. Muse Ember aims to serve as a fast, low-cost foundation for AI agents performing high-throughput, repetitive tasks, with potential to complement larger models like Muse Wonder for more complex problem-solving.

items.title: Developer warns AI-generated codebases tend to be fragile and hard to maintain due to shallow tests, complexity, and reduced human understanding [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
items.summary:
A developer who recently transitioned from Meta to another large tech company reports that heavy reliance on AI for coding leads to fragile codebases that accumulate technical debt and are difficult to maintain. The developer observed that AI-generated code often includes shallow test coverage, overly complex structures, and faster pull requests that reduce code quality and human comprehension.

The developer outlines four main issues with AI-generated code: simplistic tests that miss critical cases, unnecessary complexity from rigid adherence to coding guidelines, diminished human understanding of the codebase, and rapid code changes that outpace thorough review. These factors contribute to more frequent and prolonged incidents in AI-driven projects, raising concerns about the sustainability of AI-centric software development for large-scale SaaS applications.

items.title: Researchers propose topic-aware multi-task mental health classification with active learning stepwise relabeling to reduce label noise in Reddit data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Topic-Aware Multi-Task Mental Health Classification with Active Learning-Based Stepwise Relabeling for Social Media Conversations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-task mental health classification framework that incorporates topic information alongside emotion, sentiment, and mental health condition tasks, using data from Reddit mental health subreddits. They introduced an active learning-based stepwise relabeling method to refine noisy emotion and topic labels in two stages, improving classification accuracy while preventing error propagation.

The approach extends the Core Fusion Network by adding topic classification derived from therapist-client interactions and applies domain-specific transformer models like MentalRoBERTa. Experiments on over 54,000 Reddit posts showed modest improvements in mental health condition, emotion, sentiment, and topic classification metrics, indicating that including topic context and label refinement can enhance multi-task mental health detection from social media conversations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mental health conditions affect millions of people worldwide, yet many cases go undetected until they reach a critical stage. Social media platforms like Reddit have become spaces where people openly share their experiences, but the support is often provided by individuals without clinical training. Existing multi-task approaches jointly model emotion and sentiment for mental health classification but frequently rely on noisy labels generated by pre-trained models and overlook topic information as a useful signal. This paper introduces two key contributions: First, an existing Core Fusion Network framework is extended by adding Topic alongside existing Mental Health Condition, Emotion, and Sentiment Classification tasks, with topic labels derived from the therapist-client interactions in the CounselChat dataset. Second, an Active Learning-based Stepwise Relabeling approach is proposed to refine a small subset of noisy emotion and topic labels using pre-trained models in two stages: targeting medium-uncertainty samples first, followed by high-uncertainty samples. The predictions above a confidence threshold (0.7) are accepted to prevent error propagation. The experiments are conducted on the SuicideWatch and Mental Health dataset of 54,412 Reddit posts collected from five mental health subreddits, evaluating domain-specific transformer encoders including MentalBERT and MentalRoBERTa. The proposed Active Learning-based Stepwise Relabeling, when applied to Core Fusion Network with MentalRoBERTa, improves Mental Health Condition by 0.09%, Emotion by 0.51%, Sentiment by 0.35%, and Topic Classification by 1.57% over the baseline Core Fusion Network. The results suggest that the proposed framework significantly reduces label noise in multi-task mental health classification, and that topic information provides additional context.

items.title: Researchers present MixUA, a multi-granularity memory system for multi-user, multi-agent interactions that assigns lessons to appropriate scopes to balance learning and privacy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
items.summary: Researchers introduce MixUA, a memory system designed to improve multi-user, multi-agent interactions by distilling independent user-agent experiences into lessons assigned to user-agent pairs, individual users, agents, or global scopes based on benefit and privacy considerations. The system aims to enhance skill sharing while preventing private information leakage across users and agents. To evaluate MixUA, the team developed CrossLearnBench, a benchmark combining agent tasks with user preferences and privacy tests. In experiments involving five users and seven agents, MixUA increased task pass rates by up to 16 points compared to no memory and 5 points over a single global memory, retained up to 90% of user preferences, and limited privacy breaches to at most 0.02% of probes. The researchers suggest MixUA could enable scalable co-evolution of users and agents in global systems.

To evaluate MixUA, the team developed CrossLearnBench, a benchmark combining agent tasks with user preferences and privacy tests. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

items.title: Researchers propose QK-MAP, a magnitude-aware projection method for query-key representations in large language models that preserves token-specific magnitude information without normalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
items.summary: Researchers introduce QK-MAP, a new approach to constructing queries and keys in large language models that avoids traditional query-key normalization (QK-Norm) by encoding magnitude changes as bounded phase patterns using multiple learnable frequencies. This method maintains sensitivity to token-specific magnitude information, which QK-Norm suppresses, and controls query-key scale without discarding important attention selectivity and token importance signals. Experiments on models ranging from 190 million to 7 billion parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss compared to standard attention and QK-Norm methods. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

items.title: Researchers introduce PURL framework for Masked Diffusion Models to enable selective token revision during parallel text generation, improving accuracy by up to 47.4% and reducing decoding rounds by up to 8 times [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments?
items.summary:
Researchers propose Planned Unmasking-and-Revision Joint Learning (PURL), a training-based framework for Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) that integrates parallel generation with selective token revision to address inconsistent early token commitments. PURL jointly trains edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction on partially masked sequences, allowing a single forward pass during inference to decode and revise tokens. The approach shows significant accuracy improvements and efficiency gains across tasks like logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation.

The study reveals that effective token edits depend on the timing and context accumulation, with early edits influencing broader trajectories and later edits being more localized. These findings suggest that improving parallel generation performance relies on making the right token commitments revisable at appropriate times rather than simply increasing the number of revisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.

items.title: Researchers find language model capabilities degrade in a consistent order under compression and perturbation across multiple models and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
items.summary: A study applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned language models, evaluating 16 tasks to determine how individual capabilities fail under these conditions. The results showed that short-answer capabilities deteriorate in a nearly identical sequence across different random perturbations and within models under pruning and quantization, with factors like answer margin and frequency predicting this order. Fragility profiles derived from random perturbations could predict which tasks and facts are lost first due to compression and accurately forecast held-out task performance after calibration. However, this failure order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or apply to long-form tasks, indicating that while short-answer capability degradation is predictable before deployment, it varies with model type and task format.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compression can preserve a language model's average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities. Whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order is unclear. We applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned models, scoring 16 tasks in four answer formats against preregistered predictions. Short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format predicted this order. Fragility profiles measured under random perturbation predicted which tasks and facts compression removes first and, after four-task calibration, held-out task accuracy (median absolute error 0.11-0.12, against 0.20-0.21 for uniform decline); profiles borrowed from other model families did almost as well. The order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or hold for long-form tasks. Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment.

items.title: Researchers propose phrase-level speculative decoding using a small MLP head on frozen target models to improve throughput without changing the tokenizer or target model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Phrase-Level Speculative Decoding on a Frozen Target
items.summary: Researchers introduce a phrase-level speculative decoding method that predicts one- to three-word phrases as single entries using a small MLP head on a frozen target model's hidden states, aiming to increase throughput in language generation. This approach keeps the target model and tokenizer unchanged, verifies multiple candidates in one forward pass, and produces outputs identical to greedy decoding except for floating-point tie-breaking. Evaluated on an A5000 GPU, the method achieves up to 2.44x speedup on benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH-500 compared to HuggingFace's generate() function, using a draft vocabulary significantly smaller than previous methods like EAGLE-3.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoders raise throughput by banking more target tokens per forward pass, and Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark all do it the same way: more candidates that survive verification. All of them draft in the target's own vocabulary, so one node of the candidate tree is one target token, and the tokenizer makes that unit look like a constant. It is not. BPE's pretokenizer splits on whitespace before merges are learned, so no multi-word string can ever become a single token: in Qwen3-4B, "United States of America" is four tokens and no adjacent pair of them exists as one entry, so a phrase is out of reach of any method drafting in the target's vocabulary. We change the unit. A small MLP head reads the frozen target's hidden state and predicts a one- to three-word phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary; greedy longest-match expansion maps it back into the target's own tokens, and N candidates are verified in one forward pass behind a prefix-tree mask, so the change is orthogonal to tree depth and width. The target and its tokenizer stay frozen and a candidate is accepted only while it matches the target's own argmax, so the served output is identical to greedy decoding up to floating-point tie-breaking. On one A5000 at batch 1, against HuggingFace generate(), a 21.94M head (0.545% of Qwen3-4B) reaches 2.391x on GSM8K, 2.444x on MATH-500 and 1.544x on MT-Bench. Because the head's output layer is one row of 257 parameters per entry, the draft vocabulary size is the parameter budget: an 8,000-entry head is 3.434M parameters, 0.0854% of the target and 64x smaller than EAGLE-3's drafter, and keeps 92.3% of the larger head's GSM8K tokens per pass. With EAGLE-3 run on same prompts and baseline, our 21.94M head is ahead of tree-16 on both maths sets and behind tree-60 on every set.

items.title: Researchers introduce HiVe-Mem, a multimodal memory framework combining horizontal memory expansion and vertical evidence composition to improve long-term interaction in multimodal agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents
items.summary:
HiVe-Mem is a new multimodal memory system designed to enhance long-term interactions by effectively retrieving and utilizing past information. It organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors to expand semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors, while also composing query-adaptive evidence subsets from multiple forms such as summaries, captions, and raw images.

The framework's two-dimensional design broadens memory coverage and adapts evidence use per query, leading to consistent task performance improvements across base models. Experiments on three multimodal memory benchmarks show HiVe-Mem reduces token consumption by about 90% compared to the most efficient competing multimodal baselines, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness in managing heterogeneous multimodal information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.

items.title: Researchers release Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter multimodal AI model for engineering with deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering
items.summary: Micius-Flash is a new AI model designed for engineering tasks, featuring native multimodal input, deep reasoning capabilities, and a large 256K-token context window. It integrates expert models trained on semiconductor knowledge, hardware coding, and multimodal understanding through a Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation process, achieving significant performance improvements on hardware code and semiconductor benchmarks compared to similar-sized baselines. The model is connected to industrial tools like EDA and KiCad through Micius Harness, enabling applications in PCB design, chip design automation, and software development with iterative planning and debugging capabilities. The researchers have released Micius as an open-source project to support further development of AI agents in science and engineering.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter model for engineering with native multimodal input, deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window. We design the Micius data pipeline as a knowledge-tree-driven data flywheel comprising three stages: knowledge tree construction and expansion, data synthesis, and quality validation with hard-example augmentation. From this data, we train expert models for semiconductor knowledge and reasoning, hardware coding, and semiconductor multimodal understanding, along with agentic experts. Subsequently, we employ Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to supervise training on sequences generated by Micius itself, thereby integrating the capabilities of these expert models into a unified model. On more than 20 datasets with about 15K records, Micius-Flash averages 64.2% on hardware code benchmarks, 15.0 points above a same-size baseline. It scores 62.4% on a semiconductor-specific agent benchmark, exceeding the same-size baseline by 17.2 points. We further develop Micius Harness for industrial applications, connecting the model to specialized tools, including EDA tools and KiCad, as well as execution environments. Case studies in PCB design, chip design workflow automation, and software development demonstrate the model's ability to use tool execution feedback for multi-step planning, code debugging, and iterative verification. We release Micius as an open-source model to advance the development of agents for science and engineering.

items.title: Researchers present SkillCache, an execution-grounded method that compiles LLM agent skill orchestrations into reusable capsules, reducing token use by up to 81% and improving cross-model transfer [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
items.summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents use reusable skills to handle recurring requests, but each invocation requires interpreting and reconstructing the skill orchestration, which is inefficient. Researchers propose SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization technique that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, enabling fast replay and execution with minimal model intervention while retaining the original skill for recovery.

Using the Claude Code harness, SkillCache reduced token usage by 81% on 87 SkillsBench tasks with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable performance. The capsules also remained effective under controlled request variations and transferred across different open-weight models, increasing their mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing token consumption by 72-81%. This suggests that execution-grounded compilation can significantly improve efficiency and transferability in repeated skill use for LLM agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10022v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.

items.title: Researchers release AVCORP corpus and train Qwen3-8B to detect deception in Avalon game using Theory of Mind and communication theory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
items.summary: Researchers developed AVCORP, a corpus of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 Avalon deception games, including 37 tactics and reasoning traces with abductive hypotheses and nested Theory of Mind beliefs. They trained the Qwen3-8B model on AVCORP and evaluated it on 25 held-out games and 20 human-played games, where it outperformed untrained baselines and several leading models, matching Claude Opus 5.5 on held-out games and exceeding untrained models in F1 score on human games. This work demonstrates the potential of combining communication theory and Theory of Mind reasoning to improve deception detection in large language model-based agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today's LLM-based agents are vulnerable to deception by users and other agents. Defending against deception requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning to infer the beliefs and goals of others as well as modeling tactics based on communication theory. To enable training models to detect deception, we adopt the well-known deception game, Avalon. We present a corpus, AVCORP, of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 games of Avalon. AVCORP includes (1) 37 tactics mapped to a 4x4 behavior matrix, and (2) reasoning traces capturing abductive hypotheses, suspicion levels, and nested ToM beliefs. We train Qwen3-8B on AVCORP and evaluate it on 25 held-out games and 20 games played by humans. On held-out games, our best trained detector outperforms its untrained baseline and frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), matching Claude Opus 5.5. On human games, every trained detector exceeds the untrained model in F1 score across all rounds.

items.title: Researchers introduce SituRecBench to evaluate vision-language models as situated recommendation assistants in 3D shopping environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark designed to assess vision-language models (VLMs) acting as recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. The benchmark simulates real-world shopping scenarios, requiring assistants to engage in multi-turn dialogue, elicit user preferences, ground recommendations visually, and guide users through spatial navigation.

SituRecBench evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified protocol. Experiments reveal ongoing challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in integrating global context with local observations. This benchmark aims to advance the development of situated recommendation assistants capable of operating effectively in physical environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.

items.title: Researchers find large language models understand time rules but struggle with duration prediction and time cost awareness, revealing cognitive blind spots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers evaluated large language models (LLMs) on their temporal competence, finding that while LLMs accurately understand time-related rules from text, they significantly underestimate task durations and fail to recognize which tasks take longer to complete. The study showed that LLMs' duration estimates are influenced by event wording, amplifying human-like biases, and some models ignore substantial increases in response time when answering queries. These findings highlight challenges for LLMs in reasoning about time, a dimension they cannot directly experience, and reveal limitations in their cognitive abilities that humans typically take for granted.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand---in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5\%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5\% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3$\times$. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.

items.title: Researchers identify three key pitfalls in evaluating multi-agent collusion monitors, showing probes often detect instructions to collude rather than actual collusion decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed activation probes used to detect secret collusion among large language model agents and found that these probes primarily identify when an agent was instructed to collude, not when it independently decided to do so. Their benchmark included thousands of episodes with agents who received collusion instructions but refused to collude, revealing that published detectors struggle to distinguish between instructed colluders and refusers. The study also uncovered two additional pitfalls inflating reported detection accuracy, such as scoring after votes and lack of public argumentation by colluders in many cases.

The team demonstrated that probes trained on agents' own choices could better detect actual collusion decisions, achieving moderate accuracy even without instruction signals, and that probes could identify colluders whose goals were fine-tuned into model weights with high accuracy. They proposed a testing protocol for collusion monitors and adapted scan statistics into an online monitoring method suitable for groups of any size, aiming to improve the reliability of collusion detection in multi-agent systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.

items.title: Researchers present SPARCLING, an LLM-based pipeline generating diverse synthetic clinical discharge letters with exact PHI annotations to benchmark and improve de-identification models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generating Diverse and Verified Synthetic Clinical Notes with Labels by Construction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SPARCLING, a pipeline using large language models to generate synthetic clinical discharge letters with precise protected health information (PHI) span annotations. This approach addresses the need for challenging, diverse, and clinically plausible benchmarks to evaluate de-identification models under strict privacy regulations in the clinical domain. SPARCLING combines structured attribute sampling, template generation, and red teaming to produce diverse PHI-labeled data, demonstrating superior content diversity compared to existing public datasets.

Experiments show SPARCLING's utility as a benchmark to identify failure modes of de-identification systems in the German clinical context. Additionally, training de-identifiers on SPARCLING's synthetic data yields better performance than training solely on limited public datasets. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under strict privacy regulations in the clinical domain, de-identification is necessary to enable the use of clinical data such as for natural language processing. However, we currently lack sophisticated ways to tell which de-identification models actually are suitable. Specifically, we need benchmarks that are challenging, diverse, and clinically plausible, all while ensuring label correctness. To this end, we present SPARCLING, an LLM-based pipeline to generate synthetic discharge letters with character-exact PHI span annotations. Our pipeline combines structured attribute sampling, template generation, and red teaming to obtain diverse PHI-labeled discharge letters. In our experiments, we demonstrate this superior content diversity over existing public datasets. Further, we show SPARCLING's downstream utility as a benchmark to uncover failure modes of de-identifiers in the German clinical domain. Finally, our experiments show that training on our synthetic data can yield more capable de-identifiers than training on the scarce public data alone. Our code is available at https://github.com/Matt00n/phi_discharge_letter_generator.

items.originalTitle: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
items.summary: Researchers introduce Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that enhances Large Language Models' (LLMs) ability to select appropriate functions and generate correct arguments by combining local schema validation with decision-model verification. DM-Call accumulates verification data across attempts and uses a hybrid feedback system to iteratively refine function calls without executing external tools. Extensive evaluations on BFCL and API-Bank datasets show that DM-Call improves function-calling accuracy compared to direct generation, with only modest additional computational cost.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.10977v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

items.title: Researchers find system prompts influence large language models' willingness to refuse unsafe requests more than their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe inputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: System Prompts Affect Response Bias More Than Discriminability in LLM Safety
items.summary:
A study evaluated 13 large language models across multiple safety benchmarks and prompt types to understand how system prompts affect model behavior. Using signal detection theory, researchers found that while models vary in their ability to discriminate safe from unsafe requests, system prompts mainly shift their response bias—making them more or less willing to refuse requests—rather than improving discriminability.

The study also showed that increasing prompt clarity increases refusal rates without reliably enhancing discrimination between safe and unsafe inputs. Additionally, different prompt families influenced models to adopt various behavioral policies beyond refusal, such as seeking clarification or providing safe help. These findings suggest that system prompts primarily alter how models respond to safety-related requests rather than consistently improving their safety discernment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model safety evaluations often focus on a compliance-refusal tradeoff: models should refuse unsafe requests without refusing safe ones. We argue that this misses a broader form of prompt-conditioned task selection, where the same request can elicit different behaviors depending on the system prompt. We investigate this using a controlled evaluation crossing eight safety-task prompt families with three clarity levels across HarmBench, XSTest, and IHEval. Holding benchmark items fixed, we evaluate 13 models and use signal detection theory to distinguish two possibilities: whether models become better at telling safe from unsafe requests (discriminability), or simply more willing to refuse (response criterion). We find substantial differences in discriminability across models, but system prompts primarily shift the willingness to refuse, with smaller and less consistent effects on discriminability. Increasing prompt clarity makes models more willing to refuse without reliably improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe requests. Beyond refusal, prompt families also shift responses among six distinct behavioral policies, including clarification and safe help. Together, these findings show that system prompts primarily change how models respond to safety-relevant requests rather than consistently improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe ones.

items.title: Researchers propose quality-constrained spectral selection for cross-task model merging, improving joint success rates across six checkpoints and 21 task pairs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Are Nearby Experts Composable? Cross-Task Model Merging in Neural Thickets
items.summary:
Researchers investigate the composability of neural network experts generated by random perturbations around a shared checkpoint, finding that proximity and orthogonality alone do not guarantee successful model merging. They introduce a quality-constrained spectral selection method that combines cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, and fallback mechanisms to improve joint task performance.

Testing across six checkpoints, 21 task pairs, and five perturbation pools, the method outperforms Top-1 averaging and other ranking approaches, achieving up to 53.1% joint success for models with at least 1.5 billion parameters. Despite improvements, the study notes that composability remains conditional, with some regression and abstention observed, indicating challenges in reliably merging experts for multiple tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random perturbations around a shared checkpoint can produce experts for distinct tasks, but shared origin does not ensure that their gains survive composition. We formulate expert-pair selection for joint base-relative retention, measured by strict joint success and worst-task gain with unconditional abstention accounting. An exact finite-difference decomposition and an arbitrarily small orthogonal counterexample show why proximity and orthogonality alone are insufficient. We instantiate this formulation with quality-constrained spectral selection, a fixed-budget framework combining cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, and Base fallback. Across six checkpoints, 21 task pairs, and five independent perturbation pools, the procedure improves strict joint success over Top-1 averaging throughout and leads the four-method model-scale comparison on four of six checkpoints. For the five models with at least 1.5B parameters, matched quality-only, global-cosine, and spectral ranking attain 49.1%, 50.5%, and 53.1% joint success. Under this matched protocol, the spectral selector also yields the highest worst-task gain and Weak Pareto rate and the lowest regression rate. Mean worst-task gain reaches +0.61 percentage points, while 17.1% regression and 13.0% abstention show that composability remains conditional. Project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Thickets-Merge/.

items.title: Researchers introduce SGA-Sparse to train native SwiGLU gates for activation-sparse and low-bit LLMs, achieving up to 85% FFN channel sparsity with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers present SGA-Sparse, a method that trains native SwiGLU gates as top-k routers to convert pretrained LLaMA models into activation-sparse models with 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while maintaining zero-shot accuracy within 0.2-2.7 percentage points of dense checkpoints. The approach updates all model parameters end-to-end without adding auxiliary router parameters and preserves the original SwiGLU activation.

After training on approximately 30 billion tokens, models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters demonstrate significant sparsity gains. The study also explores quantization-aware training (QAT) techniques to mitigate performance degradation from post-training quantization, with continued-QAT recovering performance at 4-bit weights and joint-QAT improving results for sub-4-bit quantization. The researchers translate sparsity-induced weight traffic reduction into equivalent bit-widths, establishing new accuracy-traffic trade-offs that outperform existing dense low-bit quantized models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.

items.title: Researchers propose TLRS-DPO to enhance Direct Preference Optimization with token-level risk scoring for improved alignment and safety in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TLRS-DPO: Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization
items.summary: Researchers introduce TLRS-DPO, a method that augments Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) by adding token-level risk scoring to better identify and suppress unsafe or undesirable local patterns in large language model outputs. This approach remains fully offline and reference-based, incorporating a robust compensation term, a curriculum-style training schedule, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that targets high-risk tokens rather than entire sequences. Empirical results show that TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-related behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to existing DPO methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a simple and widely used alternative to RLHF for aligning large language models (LLMs), but its sequence-level objective cannot precisely locate or suppress the local patterns that make an otherwise acceptable response unsafe or undesirable. We propose TLRS-DPO (Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization), which augments DPO with fine-grained token-level control while remaining fully offline and reference-based. TLRS-DPO introduces a token-level robust compensation term that converts the policy-reference log-ratio on rejected responses into localized risk scores, a curriculum-style schedule that gradually increases the strength of this compensation during training, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that selectively penalizes only high-risk tokens instead of entire sequences. This design bridges sequence-level preference fitting and token-level behavior control, and can be implemented as a drop-in modification to standard DPO trainers. Empirically, TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-relevant behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to strong DPO baselines.

items.title: Researchers test AI agent self-improvement using failure traces with frozen 9-billion-parameter model, finding limited accuracy gains in customer-service tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated whether an AI agent's surrounding notes, written by a larger teacher model, could improve performance by learning from the agent's failure traces while keeping the agent's weights fixed. They found that notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4 percentage points in generated customer-service decisions compared to notes without failure information, but showed no improvement in full customer-service conversations. A process of selecting better-scoring notes accounted for about 60% of the total improvement observed.

Further tests screened lessons for customer-service and tool-use tasks, with mixed results: two customer-service lessons awaited new data testing, and one tool-use lesson showed no gain despite being written without failure information. A neutral note without procedures outperformed the learned lessons in exploratory tests. Additionally, a blind audit found that 146 of 240 tool-use test items were defective, highlighting challenges in evaluating tool-use improvements.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

They found that notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4 percentage points in generated customer-service decisions compared to notes without failure information, but showed no improvement in full customer-service conversations. A process of selecting better-scoring notes accounted for about 60% of the total improvement observed.

Further tests screened lessons for customer-service and tool-use tasks, with mixed results: two customer-service lessons awaited new data testing, and one tool-use lesson showed no gain despite being written without failure information. A neutral note without procedures outperformed the learned lessons in exploratory tests. Additionally, a blind audit found that 146 of 240 tool-use test items were defective, highlighting challenges in evaluating tool-use improvements.

items.summary: Researchers propose a deep reinforcement learning method for user plane function (UPF) selection in 5G networks that uses large language models to translate operator intents and network alerts into a dynamic, multi-objective reward function. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: User plane function (UPF) selection in 5G networks is an active area of research, with various limited approaches proposed to enhance network efficiency and manage resources effectively. items.title: Researchers present ODSA, an LLM-directed test-time scaling framework that orchestrates multiple solution discovery and aggregation to improve language model accuracy by up to 18 points [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ODSA: Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation
items.summary:
Researchers introduce ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), a framework where an orchestrator language model directs stateless workers to discover, compare, and verify solutions during test-time scaling to enhance language model accuracy. Unlike traditional methods that either revise a single solution or generate independent solutions in parallel, ODSA uses an orchestrator to allocate computation and integrate previous results for informed decision-making.

ODSA demonstrated improvements of 4.7 to 18.0 accuracy points across three models on the Humanity's Last Exam benchmark and 0.6 to 14.0 points on LiveCodeBench, where single direct calls already solve most problems. The orchestrator itself does not solve problems but manages the process to optimize inference outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling improves the accuracy of a language model's answers by spending more computation at inference time. Established methods do so either sequentially, revising a single solution over several passes, or in parallel, generating several independent solutions and selecting among them. We present ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), an LLM-directed scaling framework in which an orchestrator LLM is given existing test-time scaling methods as actions --- discovery of a new independent solution, comparison of existing solutions to build a better one, and acceptance of a proposed answer, which triggers its verification --- and directs stateless workers to carry them out. The orchestrator does not solve the problem itself: it allocates computation, feeds the results of earlier actions into later ones, and takes every action from a single context, so that each decision is informed by everything tried before. On Humanity's Last Exam, ODSA improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points across three models over a single direct call to the model with no test-time scaling. On LiveCodeBench, where a single direct call already solves most problems, it improves accuracy by 0.6 to 14.0 points.

items.title: Researchers propose naive LLMs intentionally deprived of topic knowledge to enhance creativity, showing 1B and 7B models generate more novel ideas refined by mentor models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Value of Not Knowing: How Fresh Eyes through Naive LLMs Fuel Creativity
items.summary:
Researchers propose naive large language models (LLMs) that are intentionally deprived of specific topic knowledge to foster creativity by avoiding existing biases and dogma. These naive models generate novel and useful seed ideas, which are then refined by stronger mentor models into concrete proposals, demonstrating that less information can lead to more innovative solutions.

The study tested 1 billion and 7 billion parameter models, finding that naive models consistently outperform baseline counterparts in producing fresh perspectives. This approach challenges the prevailing trend of scaling up training data, suggesting that intentional ignorance in LLMs can help discover genuinely outside-the-box solutions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.11725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many major scientific advances come from approaching a problem with a new or novel perspective. While large language models (LLMs) with internet-scale knowledge seem poised to take such perspectives, their consistent generation remains elusive. Instead, models are drawn to dominant views and preexisting, in-field bias. To explore the potential of fresh eyes to increase creativity, this paper proposes naive LLMs, models that are made intentionally ignorant of a specific topic. Through deprivation in training or intentional forgetting, naive models are unburdened by existing dogma, allowing them to be free to make new associations and conjectures. These naive models can then be paired with a stronger mentor model that can refine their unique perspectives into concrete proposals. For the 1B and 7B models tested in this paper, naive models consistently produce seed ideas that are more novel and useful than baseline counterparts, and mentor refinement improves the ideas even further. Thus, contrary to the prevailing tradition of scaling up training data, we demonstrate a case where less information is actually more powerful, in particular when the aim is to discover genuinely outside-the-box solutions.

items.title: Researchers propose Speculative Self-Distillation to improve language model knowledge internalization with 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and better retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), a method for training language models to internalize new knowledge efficiently by combining student-generated rollouts with selective teacher interventions. SSD aims to keep training behavior close to test-time conditions while avoiding low-signal states that hinder learning.

SSD was evaluated on three closed-book question-answering benchmarks focusing on fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, where it nearly matched the accuracy of on-policy distillation but used significantly fewer supervised tokens. Additionally, SSD outperformed off-policy distillation and demonstrated superior retention and in-domain accuracy in a forgetting stress test, establishing a new balance between accuracy, efficiency, and forgetting for self-distillation methods.
items.description:

SSD aims to keep training behavior close to test-time conditions while avoiding low-signal states that hinder learning.

SSD was evaluated on three closed-book question-answering benchmarks focusing on fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, where it nearly matched the accuracy of on-policy distillation but used significantly fewer supervised tokens. Additionally, SSD outperformed off-policy distillation and demonstrated superior retention and in-domain accuracy in a forgetting stress test, establishing a new balance between accuracy, efficiency, and forgetting for self-distillation methods.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.
