items.title: Researchers find dense reward signals improve multi-turn clinical agent training over outcome-only rewards, reducing premature decisions and supporting high-risk cases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
items.summary:
Researchers studied reinforcement learning in clinical multi-turn agents tasked with information gathering and decision-making in medication refill triage, acute diagnostics, and dosing titration. They found that using dense rewards that credit uncertainty reduction leads to better performance and fewer failures on rare high-risk cases compared to outcome-only rewards. Outcome-only training often caused premature commitment and poor handling of complex cases.

The study introduced controlled environments with hidden clinical states and exact outcome verifiers to evaluate different reward strategies. Separating exploration from exploitation further improved support for high-risk cases but increased unnecessary information gathering in low-acuity scenarios. The optimal reward design varied by task, and reinforcement learning did not reliably fix rare behavior issues inherited from biased supervised data.

These findings suggest that relying solely on verifiable final outcomes is insufficient for training reliable multi-turn clinical agents. Reward design must consider the information-gathering process, and evaluation should distinguish adaptive questioning from shortcuts that exploit reward structures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.

items.title: Researchers present Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a selective fine-tuning method for large language models that improves performance while maintaining stability using acceptance criteria [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: APE: Selective Fine-tuning with Acceptance Criteria for Language Model Adaptation
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a fine-tuning approach for adapting large language models that systematically tests multiple parameter updates on small data subsets and accepts only those that improve performance beyond a threshold. This method aims to prevent destabilizing changes common in standard fine-tuning by applying a filtered selection process inspired by evolutionary optimization.

APE demonstrated a 33.9% BLEU score improvement and a 36.2% reduction in perplexity on news summarization tasks while requiring minimal computational resources. The approach offers a practical framework for controlled model adaptation that balances performance gains with representational stability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.19912v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a selective fine-tuning method for adapting large language models that systematically explores parameter modifications while maintaining model stability. Inspired by evolutionary optimization principles, APE evaluates multiple candidate parameter updates through fine-tuning on small data subsets and accepts only those exceeding a performance threshold. Unlike standard fine-tuning that follows single gradient directions, APE implements a filtered selection process that prevents destabilizing parameter changes while enabling systematic improvement. Our method achieves 33.9\% BLEU improvement and 36.2\% perplexity reduction on news summarization tasks while using minimal computational resources. The approach provides a practical framework for controlled model adaptation that balances performance gains with representational stability.

items.originalTitle: Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers
items.summary: Reinforcement learning in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models often suffers from instability due to discrepancies between training and inference routing mechanisms, sometimes causing training collapse. Researchers identify that routing behaviors can differ significantly between these phases and even across repeated forward passes under identical conditions. To address this, they introduce Rollout Routing Replay (R3), a method that records routing distributions during inference and replays them during training to reduce policy divergence and stabilize training without slowing it down. Extensive experiments demonstrate that R3 prevents training collapse and outperforms existing methods like GSPO and TIS, offering a promising solution for stabilizing reinforcement learning in MoE models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.11370v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial approach for enhancing the capabilities of large language models. However, in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the routing mechanism often introduces instability, even leading to catastrophic RL training collapse. We analyze the training-inference consistency of MoE models and identify a notable discrepancy in routing behaviors between the two phases. Moreover, even under identical conditions, the routing framework can yield divergent expert selections across repeated forward passes. To address this foundational inconsistency, we propose Rollout Routing Replay (R3), a method that records routing distributions from the inference engine and replays them during training. R3 significantly reduces training-inference policy KL divergence and mitigates extreme discrepancies without compromising training speed. Extensive experiments on various settings confirm that R3 succeeds in stabilizing RL training, preventing collapse and outperforming methods such as GSPO and TIS. We believe this work can offer a new solution for stabilizing RL in MoE models.

items.title: IntPro introduces selective retrieval from user history to improve context-aware intent inference in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: IntPro: Context-Aware Intent Inference via Selective Retrieval from User History
items.summary: IntPro is a proxy agent designed to enhance large language models' ability to infer user intent by selectively retrieving relevant records from a user's interaction history. It decides when to retrieve past context-to-intent patterns and generates natural-language intent explanations to guide retrieval, improving disambiguation of current user goals when context alone is insufficient. The system is trained through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to jointly optimize intent prediction and retrieval decisions. Experiments across multiple scenarios and model backbones show that IntPro consistently improves intent inference accuracy by leveraging historical user data effectively.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.03325v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurately understanding user intent in context is essential for large language models (LLMs) to provide effective assistance. However, observed behavior may support multiple plausible intents, making the current context alone insufficient for identifying the user's underlying goal. A user's interaction history may contain recurring context-to-intent patterns that help disambiguate the current intent. Leveraging such historical patterns requires deciding whether to invoke retrieval for the current context and, if so, forming queries that express plausible intents rather than relying on contextual similarity alone. We present IntPro, a proxy agent that learns to either infer intent directly from the current context or generate candidate intent explanations to retrieve intent-aligned records from the user's history. We design intent explanations as a shared intent-oriented natural-language form that expresses the observed action, its functional goal, and a cue-to-intent rationale. Label-conditioned explanations represent historical records, while candidate explanations generated from the current context serve as retrieval queries in the same form. IntPro first learns direct and retrieval-conditioned inference through Direct-and-Retrieval supervised fine-tuning (SFT). IntPro then uses multi-turn GRPO with a retrieval-decision reward to jointly optimize intent prediction and selective retrieval mechanism. Experiments across three scenarios and three model backbones demonstrate that IntPro consistently improves context-aware intent inference.

items.title: Researchers propose sequential Monte Carlo method for ensembling language models to improve text generation by aggregating predictions at the string level [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Ensembling Language Models with Sequential Monte Carlo
items.summary: Researchers introduce a unified framework using sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to ensemble multiple language models (LMs) by treating ensembling as an inference problem. Their approach enables sampling from ensemble distributions in a shared byte space, accommodating models with different vocabularies and allowing consistent sampling in the limit. They evaluate various ensemble strategies across prompts and model combinations, finding that consensus-seeking methods like the product outperform simple probability averaging and that improved posterior approximations enhance ensemble performance.

Their approach enables sampling from ensemble distributions in a shared byte space, accommodating models with different vocabularies and allowing consistent sampling in the limit. They evaluate various ensemble strategies across prompts and model combinations, finding that consensus-seeking methods like the product outperform simple probability averaging and that improved posterior approximations enhance ensemble performance.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.05432v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Combining the predictions of multiple models is one of the most effective strategies in machine learning. Thus, it is only natural to investigate the ensembling of language models (LMs). However, because LMs define distributions over strings, a proper ensemble requires aggregating predictions at the string level, which requires a computation that is generally intractable. In this work, we cast LM ensembling as an inference problem and propose the deployment of sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), an appropriate approximate inference scheme. Concretely, we introduce a unified framework for composing multiple LMs into ensemble distributions parameterized by a broad family of aggregation functions. To sample from these distributions, we introduce an SMC algorithm that operates in a shared byte space, enabling ensembles of models with mismatching vocabularies and consistent sampling in the limit. We evaluate a range of ensembles across prompt and model combinations for various text generation tasks, finding that consensus-seeking strategies such as the product consistently outperform probability averaging, and that better posterior approximations can yield better ensemble performance.

items.title: Researchers find language models trained on fixed counterfactual explanations produce introspective explanations aligned with their evolving behaviors across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Introspective Coupling: Self-Explanation Training Tracks Behavioral Change Despite Fixed Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers studied language models trained to explain which input features influenced their predictions using fixed counterfactual behavior supervision. They found that these models often generate explanations more faithful to their current behavior than to the original training targets, a phenomenon termed "introspective coupling." This occurs when training explanations remain correlated with the models' behaviors despite behavioral shifts during training.

The study showed that introspective coupling tracks behavior changes even when explanation training is combined with other post-training objectives, without needing updated supervision. This effect was observed across multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and was robust to label noise. The findings suggest that fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can provide scalable, generalizable post-training signals for improving model introspection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32038v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When does training language models (LMs) to generate explanations of their predictions yield faithful introspection, rather than superficial imitation? We study LMs trained to explain which features of their inputs influenced their behavior, using models' counterfactual behavior on modified inputs as supervision. Surprisingly, we find that LMs trained on fixed counterfactual explanations derived from their earlier checkpoints, or even from behaviorally similar models in different families, frequently produce explanations more faithful to their own current behaviors than to those of their training targets. This "introspective" coupling between LM explanations and behaviors occurs when training explanations remain sufficiently correlated with current behaviors over the course of training, even as behaviors themselves shift. We also show that introspective coupling tracks behavior shifts: when explanation training is provided concurrently with other post-training objectives, explanations change to match without requiring updated supervision. This phenomenon appears in multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and is robust to label noise. Overall, our results show that even fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can provide scalable and generalizable post-training signal for introspection.

items.title: Researchers propose NeuroActiSep method to detect factual hallucinations from feed-forward neurons in a single forward pass of large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NeuroActiSep: Detecting Factual Hallucinations from Feed-Forward Neurons in a Single Pass
items.summary: Researchers introduce NeuroActiSep, a method that ranks feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token to detect hallucinations in large language models during the first forward pass. They use a neuron selection dataset from CounterFact to identify neurons correlated with hallucination and transfer these to train classifiers on other factual question-answering datasets. The study finds that probes trained on sparse sets of selected neurons perform comparably to those trained on full internal representations. The analysis also reveals that hallucination-related signals are distributed across many neurons, with random neuron sets performing well at larger budgets, while selection benefits extremely sparse neuron sets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.14448v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hallucination in large language models reduces their reliability and slows adoption. Various white-box studies have used internal representations to detect patterns of truthfulness and factuality. A less-studied approach is to identify feed-forward neurons correlated with hallucination. In this empirical study, we propose a method to rank feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token and use it to investigate the feasibility of utilizing them for hallucination detection in the first forward pass. Using a neuron selection dataset built from CounterFact for identifying neurons correlated with hallucination, we transfer the selected neuron identities to train hallucination classifiers on other factual question-answering datasets. Our work provides empirical evidence that probes trained using the features from sparse sets of selected neurons perform on par with probes trained on internal representations. We also analyze the distribution of selected neurons and the effects of layer depth and neuron budget on detection performance. Our results show that randomly drawn neuron sets are also competitive at larger budgets, suggesting that signals correlated with hallucination are distributed across many neurons, while selection can help in extremely sparse sets.

items.title: Researchers introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence metric to measure and improve consistency in large language model agents using tool use across independent runs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents that use tools can behave inconsistently when run multiple times from the same initial state, leading to different tool calls, contradictory outputs, and divergent strategies. This inconsistency grows over time and reduces reliability, while existing evaluation metrics focus mainly on task correctness and do not capture behavioral consistency across executions. Researchers propose Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from reinforcement learning bisimulation metrics, which measures cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistencies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33012v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies.This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

items.title: Survey examines mechanistic interpretability methods for AI safety, assessing their ability to understand, predict, and control neural network behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
items.summary: This survey explores mechanistic interpretability as a means to understand the internal workings of neural networks to improve AI safety. It reviews foundational concepts such as features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and evaluates methods for feature extraction, circuit discovery, causal verification, and training-data attribution. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08438v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

items.title: Researchers compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder showing label wording augmentation improves accuracy on unfamiliar words but not on abbreviations or codes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated two versions of Ru-Jev, a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks, to assess the impact of label wording augmentation on model accuracy. The later release introduced multiple surface forms for labels, and tests with various label vocabularies showed improved accuracy on ordinary and borrowed words, including jargon and slang, but no gains on abbreviations or opaque codes.

The study held questions constant while varying label wording across ten vocabularies and found that the augmented model outperformed the earlier version on most ordinary word vocabularies, with statistically significant improvements. However, on abbreviations unrelated to training and opaque codes, the augmented model's performance did not improve and sometimes declined. Additional tests on unseen datasets showed mixed accuracy changes, which could be partially corrected by fitting additive biases. The researchers also identified four evaluation hazards when comparing the two model releases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08439v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24; eleven differences survive a Holm correction and eight have a label-level interval that excludes zero. Two runs trained by mistake without the transliterated label forms stay at the earlier release's level on jargon. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: on the 17 abbreviations unrelated to training it is lower (-0.060, Holm p=0.017), and on opaque codes it stays near chance once labels related to training options are removed. With eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points; one additive bias per option, fitted on half of the rows, narrows these to -3.4 and +1.4 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

items.title: Researchers confirm emergent misalignment in nine open-weights LLMs, with misalignment rates up to 0.74% and format-dependent vulnerabilities doubling rates under JSON output [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
items.summary: Researchers evaluated emergent misalignment—a broad misalignment effect from fine-tuning on narrow, misaligned data—in nine modern open-weights large language models (LLMs) including Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families ranging from 1B to 32B parameters. They found misalignment rates of 0.74% in models fine-tuned on insecure code generation, significantly lower than the 20% observed in GPT-4o, and identified that requiring JSON output doubled misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts, especially in the Gemma 3 family. This suggests that structural output constraints may bypass safety training by limiting the model's ability to refuse unsafe outputs, confirming emergent misalignment as a reproducible but less severe phenomenon in open-weights models compared to proprietary systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.20104v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales. We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%. We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse. These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.

items.title: Researchers propose agnostic framework for language identification and generation without assuming data distribution realizability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agnostic Language Identification and Generation
items.summary: Recent research challenges the common assumption that input data for language identification and generation must come from a distribution supported on a known language. The authors introduce an agnostic setup that removes this restriction, allowing for more general input data distributions. They develop new objectives for both language identification and generation tasks under this framework and achieve novel characterizations with nearly tight statistical rates. This work broadens the theoretical understanding of language processing tasks by relaxing previous constraints and providing new performance bounds.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.23258v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent works on language identification and generation have established tight statistical rates at which these tasks can be achieved. These works typically operate under a strong realizability assumption: that the input data is drawn from an unknown distribution necessarily supported on some language in a given collection. In this work, we relax this assumption of realizability entirely, and impose no restrictions on the distribution of the input data. We propose objectives to study both language identification and generation in this more general "agnostic" setup. Across both problems, we obtain novel interesting characterizations and nearly tight rates.

items.originalTitle: Linear Model Merging Unlocks Simple and Scalable Multimodal Data Mixture Optimization
items.summary: Researchers address the challenge of selecting optimal data mixtures for supervised fine-tuning of multimodal large language models by using linear model merging as a proxy to estimate mixture performance. This approach trains domain-specific experts and combines their parameters to predict effective data mixtures without costly retraining for each combination. Extensive experiments on 14 multimodal benchmarks show that merged proxy models consistently identify near-optimal mixtures, offering a scalable and efficient solution to the data mixture optimization problem. The code for this method is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.04937v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selecting the best data mixture is critical for successful Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of Multimodal Large Language Models. However, determining the optimal mixture weights across multiple domain-specific datasets remains a significant bottleneck due to the combinatorial search space and the high cost associated with even a single training run. This is the so-called Data Mixture Optimization (DMO) problem. On the other hand, model merging unifies domain-specific experts through parameter interpolation. This strategy is efficient, as it requires only a single training run per domain, yet it often leads to suboptimal models. In this work, we take the best of both worlds, studying model merging as an efficient strategy for estimating the performance of different data mixtures. We train domain-specific multimodal experts and evaluate their weighted parameter-space combinations to estimate the efficacy of corresponding data mixtures. We conduct extensive experiments on 14 multimodal benchmarks, and empirically demonstrate that the merged proxy models consistently select near-optimal mixtures. This decouples the search for optimal mixtures from the resource-intensive training process, thereby providing a scalable and efficient strategy for navigating the complex landscape of mixture weights. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/BerasiDavide/mLLMs_merging_4_DMO.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.22586v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synthetic tabular data generation has attracted growing attention due to its importance for data augmentation, foundation models, and privacy. However, real-world tabular datasets increasingly contain free-form text fields (e.g., reviews or clinical notes) alongside structured numerical and categorical attributes. Generating such heterogeneous tables with joint modeling of different modalities remains challenging. Existing approaches broadly fall into two categories: diffusion-based methods and LLM-based methods. Diffusion models can capture complex dependencies over numerical and categorical features in continuous or discrete spaces, but extending them to open-ended text is nontrivial, since they model each column as a continuous value or one of a closed set of categories, whereas text lives in an exponentially large sequence space. In contrast, LLM-based generators naturally produce fluent text, yet their discrete tokenization can distort precise or wide-range numerical values, hindering accurate modeling of both numbers and language. In this work, we propose TabDLM, a unified framework for free-form tabular data generation via a joint numerical-language diffusion model built on masked diffusion language models (MDLMs). TabDLM models textual and categorical features through masked diffusion, while modeling numerical features with a continuous diffusion process through learned specialized numeric tokens embedding; bidirectional attention then captures cross-modality interactions within a single model. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of TabDLM compared to strong diffusion- and LLM-based baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/ilikevegetable/TabDLM.

items.title: Researchers develop reinforcement learning method for diffusion language models using entropy-guided step selection and stepwise advantages, achieving state-of-the-art results on coding and reasoning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion LLMs with Entropy-Guided Step Selection and Stepwise Advantages
items.summary:
Researchers propose a reinforcement learning approach tailored for diffusion language models (DLMs), addressing challenges from intractable sequence-level likelihoods by formulating sequence generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process. Their method derives an exact, unbiased policy gradient decomposed over denoising steps and uses entropy-guided step selection and one-step denoising rewards to efficiently estimate intermediate advantages without explicit sequence likelihood evaluation.

Experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on coding and logical reasoning tasks and shows strong results on mathematical reasoning, outperforming existing reinforcement learning post-training methods for DLMs. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further study and application.

items.title: Researchers propose Sign-Certified Policy Optimization to reduce reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback by preserving advantage sign robustness during policy updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback via Advantage Sign Robustness
items.summary: Researchers identify flipped advantage signs in reward models as a key cause of reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where maximizing a proxy reward leads to degraded true quality. They introduce Sign-Certified Policy Optimization (SignCert-PO), a method that down-weights non-robust completions during policy gradient updates by certifying sign preservation against adversarial perturbations in reward model parameters. Unlike prior methods requiring multiple reward models or training data access, SignCert-PO operates solely at the policy optimization stage using only reward model parameters and on-policy completions. Evaluations on TL;DR summarization and AlpacaFarm benchmarks show that SignCert-PO consistently improves win rates over baselines and reduces reward hacking.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.02986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reward models (RMs) used in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are vulnerable to reward hacking: as the policy maximizes a learned proxy reward, true quality plateaus or degrades. We make the assumption that reward hacking is often caused by flipped advantage signs: instead of reducing the likelihood of a bad response, a flipped sign causes the update to increase it. By considering an adversarial perturbation in the RM parameter space, we can derive a certified sign-preservation radius, which is the smallest perturbation that can flip the advantage sign during policy optimization. Based on this formulation, we propose Sign-Certified Policy Optimization (SignCert-PO), down-weighting non-robust completions in the policy gradient update. Unlike prior approaches that require multiple RMs or access to the RM training data, SignCert-PO is lightweight and operates purely at the policy optimization stage using only the RM parameters and on-policy completions. On TL;DR summarization and AlpacaFarm benchmarks, SignCert-PO consistently achieves a better win rate than baselines and reduces reward hacking.

items.title: Researchers distill hallucination detection signals into transformer representations using weak supervision on LLaMA-2-7B hidden states, enabling internal detection without external verification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Weakly Supervised Distillation of Hallucination Signals into Transformer Representations
items.summary: Researchers propose a weak supervision framework combining substring matching, sentence embedding similarity, and an LLM judge to label hallucinated responses without human annotation. They create a 15,000-sample dataset from SQuAD v2 with LLaMA-2-7B generated answers and per-layer hidden states, then train five probing classifiers on these states to detect hallucinations internally during inference. Transformer-based probes achieve strong discrimination with minimal inference overhead, supporting the hypothesis that hallucination detection can be distilled into model representations without external verification.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.06277v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing hallucination detection methods for large language models (LLMs) rely on external verification at inference time, requiring gold answers, retrieval systems, or auxiliary judge models. We ask whether this external supervision can instead be distilled into the model's own representations during training, enabling hallucination detection from internal activations alone at inference time. We introduce a weak supervision framework that combines three complementary grounding signals: substring matching, sentence embedding similarity, and an LLM as a judge verdict to label generated responses as grounded or hallucinated without human annotation. Using this framework, we construct a 15000-sample dataset from SQuAD v2 (10500 train/development samples and a separate 5000-sample test set), where each example pairs a LLaMA-2-7B generated answer with its full per-layer hidden states and structured hallucination labels. We then train five probing classifiers: ProbeMLP (M0), LayerWiseMLP (M1), CrossLayerTransformer (M2), HierarchicalTransformer (M3), and CrossLayerAttentionTransformerV2 (M4), directly on these hidden states, treating external grounding signals as training-time supervision only. Our central hypothesis is that hallucination detection signals can be distilled into transformer representations, enabling internal detection without any external verification at inference time. Results support this hypothesis. Transformer-based probes achieve the strongest discrimination, with M2 performing best on 5-fold average AUC/F1, and M3 performing best on both single-fold validation and held-out test evaluation. We also benchmark inference efficiency: probe latency ranges from 0.15 to 5.62 ms (batched) and 1.55 to 6.66 ms (single sample), while end-to-end generation plus probe throughput remains approximately 0.231 queries per second, indicating negligible practical overhead.

items.title: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2605.06660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capability in solving scientific and mathematical problems, yet they struggle to produce valid and challenging novel problems -- an essential component for advancing LLM training and enabling autonomous scientific research. Existing problem generation approaches either depend on expensive human expert involvement or adopt naive self-play paradigms, which frequently yield invalid problems due to reward hacking. This work introduces VHG, a verifier-backed hard problem generation framework built upon three-party self-play. By integrating an independent verifier into the conventional setter-solver duality, our design constrains the setter's reward to be jointly determined by problem validity (evaluated by the verifier) and difficulty (assessed by the solver). We instantiate two verifier variants: a Hard symbolic verifier and a Soft LLM-based verifier, with evaluations conducted on indefinite integral tasks and general mathematical reasoning tasks. Experimental results show that VHG substantially outperforms all baseline methods by a clear margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/VHG.

items.title: A Communication-Theoretic Framework for LLM Agents: Cost-Aware Adaptive Reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Communication-Theoretic Framework for LLM Agents: Cost-Aware Adaptive Reliability
items.summary: arXiv:2605.09121v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) rely on reliability techniques such as retry, majority voting, and self-consistency developed in parallel rather than within a common analytical framework. We observe that an LLM sampled at temperature $T$ is a discrete stochastic channel $p(y \mid x)$ in the sense of Shannon's coding theory, and use this identity as the entry point for such a framework. Each of these techniques is a special case of one of six classical reliability operators: diversity combining, hybrid retransmission, iterative generator-critic decoding, rateless sampling, structured redundant verification, and difficulty-adaptive routing. Within the framework we give two closed-form results, a noise-variance threshold above which uniform averaging beats quality-weighted averaging and a contractivity criterion for generator-critic refinement, and turn each into a design rule checkable before committing compute. We further introduce a cost-aware semantic-nearest-neighbor router whose single Lagrangian knob traverses the quality-cost frontier without retraining. Across six local and cloud channel configurations, no fixed model-technique-budget choice dominates. On a 300-item hard split of MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, the router occupies the empirical Pareto frontier: at matched quality its normalized cost is $\approx$56% lower than the best fixed technique, and at matched cost it improves quality by $\approx$7% (26% over single-shot decoding). Judge-free grading of 6,900 outputs confirms that the judge tracks correctness at the item level and that the router's advantage over a fixed policy persists at most cost settings; with internal reasoning enabled, the gain of external refinement shrinks but remains significant for our incremental-redundancy operator. These results argue for consolidating reliability techniques into a single tunable layer informed by channel coding.

items.title: What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?
items.summary: arXiv:2605.18445v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Humans can approach complex visual problems by mentally simulating intermediate visual steps, rather than reasoning through language alone. Inspired by this, several works on Vision-Language Models have recently explored chain-of-thought reasoning with continuous latent tokens as intermediate visual imagination steps. In this work, we investigate how recent models leverage such latent tokens. Surprisingly, we find that model accuracy is unaffected when latent tokens are replaced by uninformative dummy tokens. This indicates that latent tokens play a minimal causal role in the model's final prediction. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyze both the training signal provided by oracle latent representations and the quality of the latent tokens generated at inference time. Our experiments reveal two crucial issues holding back latent visual reasoning: First, in most existing datasets, oracle latent tokens provide limited additional information beyond the original image and do not substantially simplify the task, leading models to ignore them during training and effectively bypassing them at inference time. When fine-tuned on a diagnostic dataset, in which latent tokens provide sufficient support for the final prediction, we show that models can causally rely on them. Second, the latent tokens produced at inference time deviate from their corresponding oracle representations, collapsing to a narrow region and preventing benefits even when the model relies on them. Overall, our findings suggest that future progress in latent visual reasoning depends on two key pillars: high-quality datasets with informative intermediate steps and more precise latent token prediction.

items.title: Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL
items.summary: arXiv:2605.28751v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A model trained with an imperfect reward in RL may learn to exploit the reward with undesired behavior. We study a controlled form of this problem in competitive programming. A program may pass small tests while violating the intended efficiency requirement on larger inputs. We construct a family of rewards that progressively relax the efficiency constraint, making the reward increasingly easy to exploit, and train separate policies. This sweep reveals a correctness-efficiency frontier. Relaxing the reward leads to less efficient programs and more resource-limit failures. Stricter rewards suppress these failures but increase correctness failures near the model's capability boundary. This frontier is also reflected in weight space. Interpolating between the resulting models reproduces the same behavioral change. More surprisingly, extrapolation in both directions further amplifies or suppresses it beyond the trained checkpoints. Extensive experiments show that this pattern holds across pure reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding, and at both 32B and 7B scales. This suggests a simple intervention for this form of reward hacking: use a loose reward to amplify the undesired behavior, use the weight-space difference to a strict-reward model as its steering vector, and then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.

items.title: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System
items.summary: arXiv:2605.31463v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the dominant architecture for frontier language models. To meet this demand, production frameworks have built optimized MoE training stacks over years of engineering effort. Yet evolving these stacks for new architectures and system optimizations remains expensive. With the rise of AI coding agents, they could automate parts of training-framework development and accelerate this evolution. But applying them to these existing frameworks carries hidden costs, invisible to today's throughput-only evaluations. We name this missing dimension agent-task efficiency (ATE): the cost of using coding agents to understand, operate, and extend a framework. Grounded in four agent-native design principles, we build PithTrain, a compact, agent-native MoE training framework supporting pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We further introduce ATE-Bench, covering real-world training-framework tasks. Our evaluation shows PithTrain achieves throughput competitive with production frameworks and higher agent-task efficiency on ATE-Bench. On new-feature tasks, PithTrain uses up to 62% fewer Agent Turns than Megatron-LM, and up to 44% and 64% less Active GPU Time than Megatron-LM and TorchTitan, respectively.

items.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2606.00671v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

items.title: An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models
items.summary: arXiv:2606.01462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Studies of human reasoning have shown that people are typically stronger at evaluating reasoning than producing it from scratch. In contrast, large reasoning models (LRMs) are trained to excel at producing long chains of reasoning to solve complex problems. How then do LRMs perform at evaluating reasons? We investigate this with the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset: math problems and solutions with trivial reasoning flaws but valid answers, designed to isolate reasoning evaluation from the confound of reasoning production. Unlike humans, who we find are only 6% worse at grading than solving such problems, we find a substantial production-evaluation gap in LRMs: frontier models score as low as 52% when evaluating VAIR solutions, despite near-perfect solution production. Why this enigma? Through chain-of-thought (CoT) analysis, we find evidence of an answer confirmation bias: LRMs often produce then check for the correct answer instead of carefully verifying each step, fabricating rationalizations even when noticing anomalous reasoning. Linear probes corroborate this, showing that while LRM activations encode some representation of valid reasoning, they fail to robustly represent VAIR solutions as invalid. Causal patching of the final answer's representations causes LRM verdicts and activations to flip at substantial rates, demonstrating that answer validity is a causal factor in models' confirmation biases. These findings indicate an outstanding limitation in dominant approaches to reasoning training, which incentivize LRMs to produce and confirm reasoning towards correct answers, but not to robustly evaluate the underlying reasons

items.title: Closing the Activation-Cone Blind Spot: Response-Time Probing and Unified Defense [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Closing the Activation-Cone Blind Spot: Response-Time Probing and Unified Defense
items.summary: arXiv:2606.29441v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Note on v2 (Nov 2026): errors found in the evaluation code mean the empirical results reported in v1 are not supported; the theoretical corollary is unaffected. Details are in the notice on page 1 and in KNOWN_ISSUES.md in the linked repository. We compare five inference-time safety paradigms (no defense, static steering, CAST, AlphaSteer, probe-gated steering) across seven instruction-tuned models (7-31B) and five attack types (GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception, prefilling, intent laundering). We derive a corollary: any defense that gates intervention on a single layer's activation alignment with a benign reference (cone, subspace, or null-space) is blind to attacks that craft activations to lie inside that reference, whether checked at prompt time or per token. For prefilling attacks we propose response-time probing, a linear probe on the hidden state at the first generated tokens combined with a halt, and compose this halt with AlphaSteer's null-space steering. We also examine whether MMLU captures steering's utility cost and how the diversity of negative training sets affects probe false-positive rates. Code, attacks, and per-sample results are released.

items.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
items.summary: arXiv:2607.02512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

items.title: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2607.03528v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as critical decision-making components in high-stakes real-world AI systems, rendering LLM reliability a foremost practical concern. In this paper, we focus on enhancing LLM reliability through selective prediction (SP), a strategy that allows an LLM to only predict for inputs where it is likely to be correct (i.e., coverage) and hence reduce the error rate (i.e., risk) on that portion of inputs---flagging the remaining inputs for future human discretion. In other words, SP improves LLM reliability by balancing the risk-coverage trade-off and enabling seamless human-AI collaboration. To integrate SP into LLMs, we focus on the LLM post-training alignment stage and propose to align LLMs with SP performance metrics, in contrast with existing LLM alignment methods that focus primarily on correctness or calibration metrics. Specifically, we propose a novel alignment framework, Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR), which targets the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC)---a popular SP performance metric---as its alignment objective. RLSR achieves substantially better risk-coverage trade-off compared to multiple alignment baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

items.title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2608.19861v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $\tau^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT 5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an independently validated workflow-level audit.

items.title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
items.summary: arXiv:2609.02302v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.

items.title: PoEM: Predicting RL Outcomes from Existing Policies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PoEM: Predicting RL Outcomes from Existing Policies
items.summary: arXiv:2609.30226v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation models are post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize specific rewards, such as helpfulness, correctness, or instruction following. This post-training process is computationally intensive, sometimes unstable, and has to be run from scratch every time the reward model changes or when we want to combine multiple rewards. We hence ask: given a new reward function, is it possible to predict the policy RL would produce without actually training on that reward? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing PoEM, a framework for predicting RL outcomes using models previously trained on other rewards. First, we build on the fact that if the new reward function can be written as a linear combination of existing ones, then the optimal policy can be expressed as a combination of the existing policies in log-probability space. Surprisingly, even in cases where the rewards are not linearly connected, we observe that policies learned through RL often span an approximately low-rank subspace across rewards. To our benefit, the weights for this combination can be estimated using only the reward or basis policy outputs on the samples. We turn these observations into an algorithm that takes post-trained models and a target reward function, and approximates the target RL policy without any additional RL training. We experimentally evaluate our approach across programmatic and learned rewards for open-ended generation, with additional experiments on math reasoning, tool calling, and image generation.

items.title: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation
items.summary: arXiv:2609.35028v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $\alpha$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.

We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $\alpha$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.

items.title: Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.37351v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling test-time computation in continuous latent spaces offers an attractive alternative to verbose token-by-token generation for multi-step deductive reasoning. However, unregularized recurrent latent updates suffer from a deliberation drift cliff when rolled out beyond training horizons, while strictly energy-conserving or symmetric message-passing dynamics cannot break parent-to-child causal symmetry or suppress cyclic modus-ponens amplification on cyclic distraction graphs. We introduce Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation (TE-BPHD), a neuro-symbolic continuous-time latent reasoning architecture that couples skew-symmetric port-Hamiltonian conservation with relation-typed non-reciprocal directional transport and monotone dissipative damping on a semantic entity-state manifold. We prove (i) unconditional input-to-state stability and exponential contraction of autonomous rollouts across arbitrary inference depths without external norm projection, (ii) strict directional DAG reachability separation over symmetric message passing, and (iii) exact cycle-suppression margins under finite cyclic horn perturbations. Across counterfactual open-world deductive benchmarks (PrOntoQA-OOD up to depth 15, ProofWriter-OWA Cyclic at depths 5-10, FOLIO-Symbolic, and Cluttr-Relational), TE-BPHD eliminates the deep-horizon drift cliff, improves depth-10 cyclic reasoning accuracy to 90.0% (+/- 0.8%) over symmetric port-Hamiltonian and standard Transformer baselines, and supports zero-retraining adaptive Lyapunov halting that reduces average solver evaluations by 44% with negligible accuracy loss.

items.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Four Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does a Harness Repair? Four Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
items.summary: arXiv:2610.05533v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit traced its gain to rows the start left unparsed and found that the caller sent reference answers as assistant turns; replication through the same pipeline missed this defect. We preregistered four studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over capped thinking in 7 of 12 cells, mainly by parsing rows the cap left unparsed, and was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases. At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 test points but were not detectably above the strongest constant label. In the third study, GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory), thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed; the fourth comparison was inconclusive on test. On exploratory Autocast, harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers on test. On the prediction tasks (14B mortality, Autocast) the harnesses ended near the constant label. The fourth study varied search-set skew and objective on CREAK and resolved Manifold questions. All its results are descriptive because render hashes were not committed before the first replication call (D001). Minority-recall estimates were lower at 80:20 than at 50:50 in all four test cells. The balanced objective and re-selection from each search's pool had higher minority- and lower majority-recall estimates in all four cells. Five of their eight minority-recall intervals included zero, as did all eight balanced-accuracy contrast intervals. This does not show that skew explains the earlier collapse.

items.title: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17623v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.

items.title: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36617v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune coordinates with per-channel scores. Trained states are nearly rank-one and bias-like, aligned with the mean write; but the output's energy spans an order of magnitude more directions. Per-channel scores see only the diagonal of the write--read operator, so they cannot select the subspace that governs the input--output map, which is a rotation of the coordinates. We therefore propose \method{}, which keeps that subspace by applying balanced truncation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Layers differ just as sharply: most are bias-dominated, while the few that carry long-range associations are the flattest and need most of their state. We therefore introduce \spar{}, which redistributes a fixed total rank budget across layers according to the Hankel spectrum. On Mamba-2 checkpoints from 130M to 2.7B, \method{}+\spar{} halves the state at an average cost of $0.3$ WikiText-2 perplexity points, against $1.6$ for GHOST, while retaining $97\%$ of the dense model's five-digit in-context recall. At a quarter of the state, giving every layer the same rank keeps $5\%$ of that recall and \spar{} $77\%$, for a $7\%$ perplexity cost.

items.title: How Many Examples, and Which Ones? A Study of In-Context Learning for Natural Language Inference [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Many Examples, and Which Ones? A Study of In-Context Learning for Natural Language Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural language inference (NLI) is a fundamental task of natural language processing and crucial for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of AI methods. Research has mostly focused on encoder or encoder-decoder architectures. However, the field of decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs) remains underexplored. While prior work has mainly investigated complex sampling and prompting techniques, the effectiveness of a minimalistic prompting approach is yet to be examined in decoder-only LLMs. In this work, we examine and provide a comprehensive benchmark of LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Phi 4) in this domain, across the MNLI, QNLI and SciTail datasets. The performance of these models was evaluated using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies with simple and direct prompts. The results of the article indicate that LLMs generally perform exceptionally well when they are provided with a simple, straightforward prompt, challenging the notion that complex prompting techniques are always required for NLI tasks. Additionally, we find that the choice of demonstration label in one-shot prompting significantly affects performance for most models, with entailment-primed examples performing best. Our findings also show that the use of a few representative examples, in the case of few-shot, produced performance comparable or superior to prompts with higher example counts, although the efficacy of the prompting techniques is model and dataset-dependent. Moreover, our simple prompting approach consistently matched or outperformed more elaborate methods such as ICS and MCQ-based prompting.

Research has mostly focused on encoder or encoder-decoder architectures. However, the field of decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs) remains underexplored. While prior work has mainly investigated complex sampling and prompting techniques, the effectiveness of a minimalistic prompting approach is yet to be examined in decoder-only LLMs. In this work, we examine and provide a comprehensive benchmark of LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Phi 4) in this domain, across the MNLI, QNLI and SciTail datasets. The performance of these models was evaluated using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies with simple and direct prompts. The results of the article indicate that LLMs generally perform exceptionally well when they are provided with a simple, straightforward prompt, challenging the notion that complex prompting techniques are always required for NLI tasks. Additionally, we find that the choice of demonstration label in one-shot prompting significantly affects performance for most models, with entailment-primed examples performing best. Our findings also show that the use of a few representative examples, in the case of few-shot, produced performance comparable or superior to prompts with higher example counts, although the efficacy of the prompting techniques is model and dataset-dependent. Moreover, our simple prompting approach consistently matched or outperformed more elaborate methods such as ICS and MCQ-based prompting.

items.title: DramaGrow: A Regime-Aware Benchmark for Auditing LLM Judges of Multi-Episode Drama [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DramaGrow: A Regime-Aware Benchmark for Auditing LLM Judges of Multi-Episode Drama
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs can now draft complete multi-episode dramas, and LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate them. Assessing the reliability of these judges is difficult because drama quality encompasses specification-backed errors, reproducible preferences, and legitimate disagreement among human raters. Most existing evaluations reduce these cases to a single score from one judge call and leave tie calibration, call-to-call variation, and the vote margin underlying the human reference unreported. We introduce DramaGrow, a regime-aware benchmark and audit protocol for AI-generated Chinese five-episode drama. The benchmark assigns verifiable constraint violations, four-of-five preferences, and within-panel disagreements to separate denominators and evidence rules. It contains 800 episodes, 120 byte-preserving interventions, and 1,155 blinded five-rater records, including a frozen extension with 114 supermajority pairs and 21 disagreement pairs. On the frozen sets of 114 preference pairs and 35 constraint interventions, the repeated absolute-score rubrics yield overlapping performance, with mean accuracies of 53.8-55.8% and three-call agreement of 29.8-32.5%, and their accuracy falls from 71.6-71.9% to 34.8-37.1% as the tie band widens. DirectPair-GLM reaches 85.1% preference accuracy, 89.5% constraint F1, and 81.9% Detect+Locate on the same items, and exact subpanel enumeration identifies four-of-five as the smallest stable human vote margin. Evaluation protocol, tie calibration, judge-call variation, and panel margin therefore affect performance as much as rubric design. We will release the specification packages, scripts, interventions, anonymized human votes and rationales, frozen judge runs, and analysis code.
